newsitem.title: USA: New drug cocktail helping ovarian cancer patients.
newsitem.headline: New drug cocktail helping ovarian cancer patients.

text.p: Ovarian cancer, one of the most deadly forms of the disease, has been fought successfully with an experimental three-drug therapy applied after surgery, researchers said on Tuesday.
Based on 60 patients given the three-drug cocktail, 70 percent were disease-free 22 months after surgery, said Eddie Reed of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, Maryland.
By comparison, previous data showed about half of women who received standard chemotherapy after optimal surgery were disease-free after 18-19 months.
Reed and other cancer experts presented their findings at a news conference set up by the Journal of the American Medical Association, which devoted this week's issue to the disease.

Reed said the experimental treatment used drugs commonly employed to combat ovarian cancer -- cyclophosphamide, paclitaxel and cisplatin, along with a protein used to help protect the bone marrow -- but was more expensive than standard chemotherapy.

He recommended women who undergo surgery have it performed by specialists trained to remove all visible tumours. He said the disease was often misdiagnosed because its symptoms were non-specific but that it was important to catch it early.
Government experts predict 26,800 women will be diagnosed with ovarian cancer this year, and more than 14,000 will die from it. The five-year survival rate is only 46 percent.
Reed said statistics showing a lower incidence of the disease in developing nations and among women who have multiple children were not conclusive.
But he cited the argument made by some that the heavy use of talc for hygenic purposes in industrialised countries may be linked to higher disease rates.
